questions.title: What is the physical intuition behind 'hyperspherical energy' in this context?
questions.question_body: The paper states that hyperspherical energy characterizes the 'pairwise neuron relationship on the unit hypersphere.' I understand that it involves the sum of similarities (like cosine similarity) between all pairs of neurons. However, I'm struggling to understand the intuition: why does this specific metric represent the 'semantic generation ability' of a diffusion model? If we keep this energy constant, what specifically are we preventing from happening to the model's knowledge?

questions.title: How does the orthogonal transformation $\bm{R}$ preserve hyperspherical energy while still allowing for finetuning?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the logic of using an orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$. If $\bm{R}$ is an orthogonal transformation, it rotates or reflects the weight vectors. If we are rotating the weights, aren't we changing the values of the weights? How can we 'change' the weights to learn a new task (like a specific subject) while simultaneously 'preserving' the hyperspherical energy? It feels like a contradiction—how can the model learn anything new if the relative angles between neurons stay the same?

questions.title: Could you explain the mathematical derivation for the $\epsilon$-deviation constraint in COFT?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.3, the paper introduces Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) where $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \leq \epsilon$. To make this differentiable with the Cayley transform, the authors use a Neumann series approximation $\bm{R} \approx \bm{I} + 2\bm{Q}$. Can someone walk me through how the constraint $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \leq \epsilon$ is mathematically transformed into $\|\bm{Q} - \bm{0}\| \leq \epsilon'$? I want to understand why the factor of 2 appears and if this approximation holds for large $\bm{Q}$.

questions.title: Why does adding a diagonal scaling matrix $\bm{D}$ in Re-scaled OFT not change the hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that re-scaling neurons does not change the hyperspherical energy because 'the magnitude will be normalized out.' The definition of hyperspherical energy $\text{HE}(\bm{W})$ uses $\hat{\bm{w}}_i := \bm{w}_i / \|\bm{w}_i\|$. If we multiply a weight vector $\bm{w}_i$ by a scalar $s_i$ from the diagonal matrix $\bm{D}$, the new normalized vector $\hat{\bm{w}}_i$ remains exactly the same. Does this mean that the 'magnitude' of the neuron weights has absolutely no impact on the semantic structure of the model, and the only thing that matters is the direction in the high-dimensional space?

questions.title: How does OFT fundamentally differ from LoRA in terms of what they 'preserve'?
questions.question_body: I am trying to compare OFT and LoRA. LoRA adds a low-rank update $\Delta \bm{W}$ to the original weights $\bm{W}^0$. OFT applies a multiplicative orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$ such that $\bm{W} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0$. The paper says LoRA 'prevents the information... from shifting dramatically' while OFT 'prevents the transform... from destroying the pretraining information.' Can someone clarify the difference? If I have a weight $\bm{w}^0$, and I add a small $\Delta \bm{w}$, the direction changes slightly. If I multiply by $\bm{R}$, the direction changes significantly but the 'angle between $\bm{w}_1$ and $\bm{w}_2$' stays the same. Why is the latter better for preserving semantics than the former?

questions.title: What is the significance of the 'sudden convergence' phenomenon in ControlNet vs. the 'smooth' convergence in OFT?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.2, the authors contrast the convergence of ControlNet with OFT. They mention that ControlNet shows 'sudden convergence' after the 8th epoch, while OFT is 'smooth and predictable.' From a deep learning optimization perspective, why does an orthogonal constraint on the weights lead to a smoother loss landscape? Is it because the optimization is happening on a manifold (the orthogonal group $\text{O}(d)$) rather than in Euclidean space?
